summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity. France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while New Caledonia legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are French national provisions that apply here as French law, and no source in this inventory records a local ordinance narrowing them. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's marriage-equality law signed 18 May 2013, following a Constitutional Council ruling of 17 May 2013; registered PACS partnerships have been available since 1999. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on the first same-sex wedding solemnised in France under that law, and PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore has the same access to marriage as any other couple.

Legal gender can be changed without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical diagnosis, under a law signed 18 November 2016 after a Constitutional Council ruling of 17 November 2016, effective 1 January 2017. An application must still be made to a court; a first-name change can be handled at a registry office.

Discrimination on the ground of "sexual identity" entered the French Penal Code in July 2012 through the sexual-harassment law, enabling prosecution of discrimination and transphobia as discrimination; the term was replaced by "gender identity" in Penal Code article 225-1 on 18 November 2016. The Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, sanction, dismissal or other discriminatory measures on that ground, and national legislation since 1985 prohibits sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services. Since 2017 transphobia has operated as an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by imprisonment.

The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic and transphobic comments with a maximum fine of 45,000 euros and/or 12 months' imprisonment, amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 on injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on sexual orientation, and raises penalties where assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation. Conversion therapy was banned by a law passed by the Senate on 7 December 2020, concurred by the National Assembly on 25 January 2022 and published on 1 February 2022, following a 2019 proposal carrying two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine.

Detention carries documented risk. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 reported that trans women in France are incarcerated according to their legal gender marker under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, so placement follows the identity document rather than anatomy and typically places them in all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by detainees; the French prison framework applies to establishments in this collectivity as French law. The French detention-places watchdog CGLPL issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding a "persistence of serious violations" of transgender detainees' rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. That opinion extends to establishments here as French law applies.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location, and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine characterised increased demand as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and a "primarily social problem" while advising extreme caution without changing practice. A bill passed by the Senate in May 2024 would ban medical transition under age 18; it has had no update since 23 July 2024, is opposed by the Macron government and is unlikely to pass the National Assembly amid large protests.
tangentialFactors:
Police in France recorded around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018, after President Macron denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France in October 2018. These are raw national counts with no population denominator, so they indicate recorded volume and reporting trends rather than a per-capita rate, and they combine homophobic with transphobic incidents rather than isolating trans victims.

The political contest over youth care is unresolved. A March 2024 report by the Little Mermaid Observatory characterised gender-affirming care for minors as a health scandal and preceded the Senate vote of May 2024; the bill has had no update since 23 July 2024. In 2022 the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, a national anti-discrimination body, was revealed as a member of that Observatory, which called the care "mutilation", prompting one committee resignation.

France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, the first country to declassify gender dysphoria, but transgender organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement.
localsOnly:
Residents must still go before a court to change legal gender, though no surgery, sterilisation, psychiatric certificate or medical diagnosis is required since the law effective 1 January 2017; a first-name change can be completed at a registry office.

In-country gender-affirming surgery has been legal since 1979. Transsexualism remains listed under ALD 31, with treatment funded by the Sécurité Sociale, and France's 2010 declassification of gender dysphoria did not alter that funding route according to transgender organisations.

The Labour Code bars discriminatory recruitment, sanction, dismissal or other measures on the ground of gender identity, and since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by imprisonment. Conversion therapy has been banned since its publication on 1 February 2022.

Care provision for minors is governed by late-2024 pediatric guidelines recommending puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2, with calcium and vitamin D supplementation. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location, and recommended moving to informed consent and self-determination.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or border-screening practice for New Caledonia, including whether gender markers on foreign passports are checked against presentation or trigger secondary screening at La Tontouta or other ports of entry. That question is unresolved here.

No source documents local New Caledonian ordinances, local enforcement practice, or incidents involving trans people in New Caledonia itself. Whether French anti-discrimination provisions and the 2004 and 2017 aggravating-factor rules have been applied in New Caledonian proceedings is not sourced.

The inventory contains no data on detention establishments in New Caledonia. The CGLPL opinion and the Article D248 placement practice are documented for mainland French establishments; their application at local facilities is inferred from the extension of French law, not directly observed.

No source records access to facilities, shelters or public services on the basis of gender presentation in New Caledonia, and no local violence statistics for trans residents are available here. The status of the Senate bill on medical transition under age 18 is unresolved after 23 July 2024.
